title: Chapter 52 — The Albatross
paragraphs: Southeastward from the Cape, off the distant Crozet Islands — a good cruising ground for Right Whalemen — a sail appeared ahead: the Goney, or Albatross by name. As she slowly drew near, from my lofty perch at the foremast-head I had a good view of that sight so remarkable to a newcomer in the far ocean fisheries: a whaler at sea, long absent from home.

As if the waves had been bleachers, this craft was whitened like the skeleton of a stranded walrus. All down her sides, this ghostly appearance was streaked with long channels of reddened rust, while all her spars and rigging were like thick branches of trees furred over with frost. Only her lower sails were set. It was a wild sight to see her long-bearded lookouts at those three mastheads. They seemed clad in animal skins, so torn and patched was the clothing that had survived nearly four years of cruising. Standing in iron hoops nailed to the mast, they swayed and swung over the deep. Three of the ship's officers leaned over the railing with long, bent fishing rods. They would not have looked very different from three old trees with three old crows perched on them.
"Ship ahoy! Have you seen the White Whale?"

But as the strange captain, leaning over the pale bulwarks, was in the act of putting his speaking-trumpet to his mouth, it somehow fell from his hand into the sea. And the wind now rising fiercely, he struggled in vain to make himself heard without it. Meanwhile his ship was still increasing the distance between us. While the seamen of the Pequod were silently acknowledging this ominous incident at the first mere mention of the White Whale's name to another ship, Ahab paused for a moment. It almost seemed as though he would have lowered a boat to board the stranger, had not the threatening wind forbidden it. But seizing his own speaking-trumpet, he knew that the other vessel was too far away to be heard, so he merely stood watching her move off, always gazing at the retreating ship as long as she remained in sight.

At that moment the two ships' wakes were crossing, and instantly — as was their strange custom — schools of small harmless fish that had been peacefully swimming alongside us for days darted away with what seemed shuddering fins, and lined themselves up alongside the stranger's flanks. Though in the course of his continuous voyaging Ahab must often have noticed a similar sight before, to any monomaniac man the most trivial things can carry powerful meanings.

"Swim away from me, do you?" murmured Ahab, gazing over into the water. There seemed little in the words, but the tone conveyed more deep helpless sadness than the mad old man had ever before shown. But turning to the helmsman, who had been holding the ship into the wind to slow her progress, he cried out in his old lion's voice — "Up helm! Keep her off round the world!"

Round the world! There is much in that sound to inspire proud feelings. But where does all that circumnavigation lead? Only through numberless dangers to the very point where we started, where those we left behind — safe and secure — were all the time ahead of us.

Were this world an endless plain, and by sailing eastward we could forever reach new distances and discover sights more sweet and strange than any Cyclades or Islands of King Solomon, then there would be promise in the voyage. But in pursuit of those far mysteries we dream of, or in tormented chase of that demon phantom that at some time or other swims before all human hearts — while chasing such things over this round globe, they either lead us on through barren mazes or midway leave us overwhelmed.
